problem: The lead says steam tables turn p₂ and T₂ into h₂ 'and then into dryness x₁', which suggests only the outlet measurements are needed. x₁ also needs the inlet pressure p₁ to get h_f1 and h_fg1. A student skimming the lead may miss this.
fix: Say: the outlet p₂ and T₂ fix h₂ from the superheated table; the inlet pressure p₁ gives h_f1 and h_fg1; together they give x₁ = (h₂ − h_f1)/h_fg1.

problem: The chapter says the throttling calorimeter fails when the outlet stays wet, but never states the practical working range. The needed superheat shrinks as the inlet gets wetter and as p₁ rises, so the instrument only works for fairly dry steam (in practice x₁ roughly above 0.95, and less at high pressure). Without this, students may think any wet steam can be tested as long as the outlet happens to be superheated.
fix: Add one line: the throttling calorimeter works only for slightly wet steam, because enough throttling superheat must remain; for very wet steam the outlet stays wet and the separating or combined calorimeter must be used.
